title: In Face of Increasingly Severe Extreme Weather: Sustainable Property Insurance under Risk

context_sources.name: Lane, Pricing risk transfer transactions, ASTIN Bulletin 2000

limitations: A MATHmodels watermark of repeated glyphs runs through every page and through the equations.
Equations 1 to 27 print with subscripts, exponents, and products split onto separate lines.
The contents page lists section 5 before section 4.
The summary calls the equilibrium model DBMI and Lane's rule the AFC model; the body says DEMI and LFC, and one chapter says DBIM.
Tables 2, 3, and 9 shift their last rows, so some numbers are not securely paired with their labels.

tasks: Decide which areas an insurer should underwrite as extreme weather worsens
Adapt the risk model so a developer can judge where, how, and whether to build
Score an uninsured landmark and recommend how far to go in preserving it
Write the community a letter with measures, a timetable, and a budget

section_map.summary: A quotation, a premium range, four areas covered, and a temple scored at 0.463.
A trillion dollars of losses and a Swiss Re forecast of 35 to 120 percent.
Four assumptions, each with a justification.
Expected loss, frequency, demand, and risk, each given a symbol.
Four hazards, an autoregressive forecast, and a premium with a loading.
A binary underwriting choice maximizing demand minus risk.
Two regions, eight areas, and a plan that covers four of them.
A willingness-risk plane and three risk adjustments.
Eight indicators, a consistency ratio of 0.058, and three bands.
A score of 0.463 and four measures against flood and cyclone.
Two strengths and two limits, one per model.
A timetable and a budget in Vietnamese dong.

contributions.summary: The premium adds Lane's loading, with its published exponents, to the expected loss.
Underwriting is reduced to a binary plan that trades total demand against total risk.
Each hazard gets its own risk adjustment: distance, structural strength, or water efficiency.
The landmark value is banded so that a score names the grade of protection.

dependency_graph.handoff: The weighted area risk becomes the horizontal axis and the input to the three adjustments.
The areas the insurer refuses are where the preservation model is applied.

assumptions.summary: An insurer bears its risk alone and does not diversify.
Insurance is a normal good, so demand falls as the premium rises.
Current development decisions ignore extreme weather.
Records from agencies and major insurers are accurate.
A landmark's value is the weighted sum of eight indicators.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: 744 Australian records since 1967 and 2021 Southeast Asian records since 1970.
Australian events regrouped into bushfire, cyclone, flood, and storm.
High-risk areas chosen from the frequency chart, with Thailand kept as an exception.
Pairwise judgments borrowed from published heritage studies.
The Temple of Literature, founded 1070, taken as the worked case.

models.summary: Prices each area and chooses which to underwrite.
Adjusts the risk of a site the developer already wants.
Scores an uninsured landmark and bands the protection it needs.

verification.summary: Differencing stops when the augmented Dickey-Fuller test says the series is stationary.
Every fit clears R squared of 0.6, and both information criteria are reported.
The judgment matrix passes with a consistency ratio of 0.058.
Protection is judged by comparing five indicators against a base of one.

results_trace.summary: The weakest fit in the table still reaches an R squared of 0.629.
Premiums run from 119.20 dollars in the Philippines to 1295.62 in Victoria.
Queensland, Western Australia, the Philippines, and Thailand are covered.
Intangible heritage receives 39.434 percent of the weight.
The temple scores 0.463, inside the moderate band.

writing_logic.summary: Open on a quotation, then reduce the task to two opposing pressures.
Give every assumption a justification, and concede what it leaves out.
Choose the formula by the wealth of the region it is applied to.
Keep an area that fails the cutoff, and say why.
Explain each acceptance and each rejection from the same table.
Match the remedy to the hazard, and say why the obvious remedy fails.
Pick the example from an area the earlier model refused.
Price every measure, explain a zero, and admit the cost that cannot be priced.

language_observations.summary: The borrowed pricing rule is credited to its author and year before its constants are used.
The demand line is given its textbook name, so the reader knows which curve it is.
A system the authors did not study is named and then set outside the work.
The undefined coefficients are conceded in the chapter's own conclusion.

visualization_observations.summary: Figure 1 maps the global impact of natural disasters.
Figure 2 draws the argument as a single flowchart.
Figure 3 groups the event types the study keeps.
Figure 4 shows the differenced New South Wales series.
Figure 5 draws the demand curve and how willingness shifts it.
Figures 6 and 7 show the regrouped categories in each region.
Figure 8 gives the frequencies behind the choice of high-risk areas.
Figure 9 overlays the fitted curves for Indonesia and Western Australia.
Figure 10 compares the premiums across areas.
Figure 11 divides the willingness-risk plane into four quadrants.
Figure 12 lays out the four dimensions and eight indicators.
Figure 13 contrasts the site with protection and without it.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: A judge rewards a decision where every accepted and rejected area is explained from the same table.
A judge penalizes a risk adjustment whose coefficients are never given values.
A judge rewards a weighting that reports its consistency ratio.

weaknesses.summary: The equilibrium model is called DBMI in the summary, DEMI in the body, and DBIM in one chapter.
Lane's pricing rule is called the AFC model in the summary and the LFC model in the body.
The demand curve is drawn but its slope and intercept are never estimated.
The Australia table shifts its last column, so Western Australia's figures are misaligned.
The development method is never applied to a real site.
The weight table's rows are shifted, so the percentages may be paired with the wrong indicators.
The preservation score grades the effort but cannot choose the measure.

independent_extensions.statement: Fit the demand slope and intercept to observed take-up before rerunning the underwriting plan.
independent_extensions.reason: The plan depends on a demand curve the paper draws but never estimates.

independent_extensions.statement: Apply the three risk adjustments to one named site and report the quadrant it moves to.
independent_extensions.reason: The development method is stated in full and then used on nothing.

candidate_rule_impacts.impact: Supports forecasting each area and hazard with its own autoregressive model before any pricing.
Supports choosing the areas to underwrite by a weighted difference of demand and risk, then reusing that risk for siting and preservation.

unresolved_questions: What slope and intercept the demand curve would have if it were fitted.
Which indicator actually carries the 39.434 percent weight, given the shifted table.
Whether any real site would cross from the high-risk quadrant to the low-risk one.
